rv.q: The mechanics of this vintage piece weren’t entirely smooth on opening night, but the intended audience here is surely after surefire laughs and glamour rather than perfect line-readings or radical reappraisal.
It’s all still pretty pointless — but always handsomely, often amusingly pointless.
Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant star in an amusing, if unadventurous revival of Noël Coward’s classic comedy
Instead it’s Ophelia Lovibond’s Sorel who emerges as the most vital character.
Despite a good cast and elegant set, it remains as shallow as its characters.
The play still amuses, but it’s a patchy evening; while Grant is great fun, Baranski is serviceable rather than sensational.
But though polished witticisms and a solid cast make for an enjoyable enough night, this Hay Fever mostly feels like it’s on period comedy autopilot.
It’s fun, but it won’t leave your eyes streaming.
Hay Fever thrives precisely on this type of frothy reliability, and Burns delivers it with style: by the book, impeccably performed, and an unalloyed autumnal treat.
At its best moments, this production of Hay Fever works like a well-oiled clock, each of its comedic elements clicking neatly into place.
Emily Burns has directed a solid production that still needs time to bed in, which it will: the famous and talented cast is enough to pull punters in.
Noël Coward’s regularly revived Hay Fever returns to the West End — and it is just as frothy and fun as ever.
A comfortable and comforting night at the theatre – just don't expect fireworks.
But the odour of mothballs is becoming inescapable.
Led by Christine Baranski’s effortless prowess, Hay Fever is not simply a good night out at the theatre, it is pure bliss.

Fusing acid barbs with immaculately timed and withering silences - matched only by moments of excruciatingly brilliant awkwardness - each of Coward's quips lands perfectly, Emily Burns having helmed a magnificent company.
Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant offer up a light and delicious West End confection.
Ridiculous, unpredictable, theatrical and just a damn good evening out.
It is a joy to watch the double Tony Award winner in action as the matriarch of this happily dysfunctional family.
This production of Hay Fever is very good indeed.
Subtle and ferocious, Coward remains our best chronicler of the family bust-up.
Coward's signature acidity is strong enough to permeate the performance, but the cast endeavours to dull its zing.
Hay Fever is brimming with wit, performed by a strong cast of comedic actors. A feel-good production with all the glamour – this Coward classic is full of joy.
Worth booking for the performances alone, even if the play itself is a little thin on substance.

cn.t: Grant and Baranski lead a polished but traditional Coward revival that delivers frothy entertainment through strong ensemble work, though critics find the production plays it safe with a lightweight, plot-thin comedy that only intermittently sparkles.
